claim: Larger LMs are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false items, and self-evaluation of open answers (P(True)) improves when the model sees many of its own samples.
quote: We study whether language models can evaluate the validity of their own claims
title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
transfer: Use P(True) over several own samples as a cheap monitoring signal before choosing to escalate.

claim: A trained P(IK) predictor (probability I know the answer) generalizes only partly across tasks and is less well calibrated on new tasks.
title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
transfer: Do not trust a pre-solve 'can I solve this' signal on a new task class until calibrated on that class.

claim: Verbalized confidence from LLMs is overconfident; sample consistency and aggregation reduce this; white-box methods beat black-box only slightly; all methods struggle on professional-knowledge tasks.
quote: As model capability scales up, both calibration and failure prediction performance improve.
title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
transfer: Prefer agreement across samples over stated confidence as the monitoring signal.

claim: Intrinsic self-correction (no outside feedback) struggles on reasoning and can make performance worse.
title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
transfer: Run revision steps only when a real external check output exists; skip pure self-critique loops.

claim: GPT-4 and Llama 2 can tell their own text from other LLMs and humans above chance, and fine-tuning shows a linear link between self-recognition and self-preference bias, causal in controlled tests.
quote: LLMs such as GPT-4 and Llama 2 have non-trivial accuracy at distinguishing themselves from other LLMs and humans.
title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
transfer: Judge candidates with a fresh call or a real check, and derive the expected answer before seeing candidates.

claim: Semantic entropy predicts incorrect answers better than baselines: mean AUROC 0.790 vs P(True) 0.698, naive entropy 0.691, embedding regression 0.687 across 30 task-model combinations; it detects confabulations, not consistent errors.
quote: proposing entropy-based uncertainty estimators for LLMs to detect a subset of hallucinations
title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
transfer: Cluster sampled answers by meaning and use cluster entropy as the trigger for extra work.

claim: A Nelson-Narens style harness (pre-solve feeling of knowing, post-solve judgment, control to trust, retry or aggregate) raised pooled accuracy of Claude Sonnet-4.6 from 48.3 to 56.9 across text, code and multimodal benchmarks; authors' claim, equal-token control not checked.
title: LLMs know when they know, but do not act on it: a metacognitive harness for test-time scaling
transfer: Closest published design to our router; replicate with an equal-token best-of-N arm.

claim: Across 20 LLMs and 10,480 evaluations, monitoring and regulation are only weakly related (r = .17, wide CI because n = 20), and accuracy rank and metacognitive sensitivity rank are largely inverted.
quote: Retrospective monitoring and prospective regulation appear separable (r = .17)
title: The Metacognitive Monitoring Battery
transfer: Do not let the model decide to act on its own error signal; a program applies the control rule.

claim: Reflexion (verbal reflections stored in episodic memory after environment feedback) reached 91% pass@1 on HumanEval vs 80% reported for GPT-4.
title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
transfer: Write a short lesson after a failed check, with real feedback, and feed it to the next try.

claim: Warmth ratings rose similarly for insight and noninsight solutions, so warmth did not distinguish them (no replication of earlier warmth findings); insight solutions were more often correct (about 57% vs 37%), but confidence did not discriminate correct from incorrect insight answers above chance.
title: Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks
transfer: A self-rated 'getting close' signal is noisy; use it only as a hint, never as a stop gate.

claim: Participants stuck more often with incorrect solutions reached by insight on a later recognition test, so a sudden confident answer can be wrongly sticky.
title: Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks
transfer: A confident first answer needs an outside check on tasks with known traps (riddles).

claim: Nelson and Narens framed metacognition as an object level and a meta level linked by monitoring (up) and control (down).
title: Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
transfer: Architecture: object-level solver calls plus a program-run meta level that monitors and controls.

claim: Testing beats restudy with a meta-analytic average of about g = 0.50 (159 effect sizes), larger with feedback; value taken from the earlier brief and my memory, not opened (publisher redirects blocked).
title: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention
transfer: Human forgetting effect; for an agent it only motivates predict-then-reveal memory, an untested guess.

claim: Self-explanation prompts help learning with overall g about 0.55 across 69 effects in 64 reports; figures from earlier brief and memory, publisher page blocked and the PDF could not be parsed.
title: Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
transfer: On failed checks, write why the candidate failed in terms of the rule using real check output.

claim: Productive failure (problem solving before instruction) beats direct instruction in a meta-analysis of 53 studies and 166 comparisons; I recall an overall g near 0.36 but did not verify the number.
title: When problem solving followed by instruction works: evidence for productive failure
transfer: Store failed attempt plus fix as a contrast pair; test showing it only after a new first attempt fails.

claim: Instruction that helps novices (worked examples, guidance) loses value or harms experienced learners: the expertise reversal effect.
title: The expertise reversal effect
transfer: Fade scaffolding by measured per-class pass rate: show nothing extra where plain already passes (our 92% word puzzles).

claim: Worked-example effect in maths: g about 0.48 over 181 effect sizes; correct examples beat incorrect ones; figure from earlier brief, not opened.
title: Meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance
transfer: Show correct worked solutions, not failed ones, as first-line guidance for classes the agent is weak at.

claim: Dunlosky et al. rated practice testing and distributed practice as high utility, and highlighting, rereading and summarization as low utility, among ten learning techniques.
title: Improving students learning with effective learning techniques
venue: Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1)
transfer: Rereading stored lessons is the weak form; retrieval-style use (predict, then reveal) is the strong form, for people only.

claim: Feeling of rightness: fluent intuitive answers feel right, and a low feeling of rightness predicts more rethinking and answer change.
title: Intuition, reason, and metacognition
transfer: Machine analogue: high agreement among samples stops thinking; low agreement or a failed check triggers more work.

claim: Experts sort physics problems by deep structure, novices by surface features.
title: Categorization and representation of physics problems by experts and novices
transfer: Route a problem by structural class (not surface text) when choosing which stored lessons to show.

claim: Gap: no controlled equal-token study of productive failure or expertise reversal applied to LLM prompting was found; web search budget ran out before a recheck, so treat as a gap, not proof of absence.
title: Search coverage note
transfer: Run our own three-arm test: bare, fixed scaffold, adaptive.
